item.title: Why columns matter. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
One of my newspaper columns changed how the British government works.
OK, changed in a pretty small way, but change it it did.
Which is a useful answer to the question posed by HM Nazmul Alam in this newspaper .
Why do we write opinion columns, why do we bother? As we say in Britain, today's newspapers are, after all, tomorrow's wrappers for the fish and chips.
We might provide some passing amusement to readers but are we actually important? Do we change the world at all?
So, an example from my own life. My writing life if you prefer.
It's an obvious observation that there are a lot of people demanding that taxes should be higher. Usually, taxes on other people should be higher.
But there are some who insist that the government having more money would make the world a better place. So, I wondered about this. I went to the UK Treasury and asked them whether anybody had made extra, voluntary, tax payments last year because they thought this way.
That no one had asked this before became clear very quickly. For no one knew. Not only that, the Treasury itself thought the idea wholly ridiculous.
It took them a few months to find out, but eventually they were able to tell me that in the tax year 2005, there had been five voluntary donations. Donations -- four of those donating were dead, leaving bequests. From which we can derive that there was one whole person in the country of the 70 million at the time who thought that the government having more money was so important that they voluntarily sent in more tax than they had to pay.
This is not grand evidence of the desire of everyone to pay more tax, of course, despite the very high number of people who demanded that taxes should be higher.
So, I wrote my column, The Times published it in 2006. I thought it was a very good joke, and I cashed my cheque for having written it.
As far as I was concerned, that was that. Well, except for dragging that example out now and again when there was one or another group demanding that they all be taxed more. For there are such groups.
Patriotic Millionaires is one of them. Rich people who demand that they be taxed more because they're rich. To which a perfectly sensible, even sufficient, answer is that you can pay extra tax, go ahead. Isn't it amazing how none of them do?
A number of people have, over the years, repeated my column, including the numbers for different tax years. I've not been keeping track but I think I'm right in saying that never has the number gone beyond a dozen of those voluntary, extra, taxpayers.
So far so, just me and my little joke. But a few weeks back, those Patriotic Millionaires demanded, again, that they be taxed more. The answer from the government was that you can pay extra tax, if you wish, and they referred to the government webpage which explains how to do it . That response, that webpage, stems directly from that column I did two decades ago.
But is it true that writing a newspaper column can indeed change the world?
Obviously, we're not going to bring about peace, love, and understanding for all forever. But it might well be possible to make a little change, here or there.
In my professional work at a think-tank, I've been a part of more substantial changes too. But yes, columns matter. And it's not the ones we think either.
I really was trying to make a joke about the difference between the public calls and the private actions, and I was doing so in order to do nothing more than gain a few pounds sterling to spend on my own desires.
One final thing. A little thing for any journalist out there interested in finance. Repeat the article for Bangladesh. We all know -- and can probably identify -- those who insist that taxes should be higher.
So, go and ask the authorities how many people pay higher than legally demanded taxes. Find out -- how many people made donations to the government last tax year? The article comparing that to how many call for higher taxes will be published. If you really work at it, you can do it anew each year too.
No, I'll not try to charge a royalty on the idea -- I stole it from an American, about the US, in the first place. They've been running an account called “Gifts to the United States” since 1843. It's never received more than a handful of millions of dollars in any one year.
People just don't believe in higher taxes enough to pay them when they don't have to. And that? That's a really useful little lesson from a newspaper column.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Revenge is not a development strategy. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Two World Bank reports, published less than 11 months apart, illustrate the increasing fragility of Bangladesh's development gains.
The November 2025 Poverty and Equity Assessment documented a decline in national poverty from 37. 1% in 2010 to 18. 7% in 2022.
The Bangladesh Development Update, released on October 6, 2026, presents a troubling reversal: National poverty is estimated at 22.5% in FY 2025-26 and projected to reach 22.8% in FY 2026-27.
The latest update also estimates that approximately 2.1 million additional people fell below the international poverty line of $3 per day during FY 2025-26.
This is a distinct measure from the national poverty rate. Both indicators point to deteriorating household welfare, although neither represents a new household survey count. This distinction is important when using these figures to assess government performance.
The central question is whether Bangladesh can pursue accountability without undermining productive businesses and the livelihoods they support. When political retaliation damages factories or obstructs legitimate commerce, workers bear costs that have not been imposed by any court.
A fair assessment requires acknowledging that the crisis did not begin in August 2024. Inflation, foreign exchange shortages, and import restrictions had already weakened the economy.
Banking vulnerabilities accumulated over many years due to weak oversight, connected lending, and governance failures. The poverty assessment also found that growth had become less inclusive after 2016. Recent global energy disruptions have added further pressure.
However, inherited conditions do not absolve the government of responsibility. Governments must be assessed on whether their actions contain existing weaknesses or exacerbate them.
The World Bank identifies financial fragility, energy constraints, weak revenue mobilization, and uncertainty as obstacles to recovery. Protecting lawful business activity and maintaining public order are essential components of an effective response.
Growth slowed from 5.8% in FY 2022-23 to 4.2% in FY 2023-24, then to 3.5% in FY 2024-25, and is estimated at 3.4% in FY 2025-26. The slowdown therefore began during the Awami League regime.
Moreover, FY 2025-26 spans both the interim and the elected government, with the latter assuming office in February 2026. Attributing the entire year's performance to either administration would misrepresent the chronology.
Nevertheless, the destruction of industrial assets after August 2024 deserves direct scrutiny. The looting and arson at Gazi Tires in Rupganj on August 25, 2024 became a disturbing example of the failure to protect a business associated with a former minister.
Reports of missing people require careful investigation; they should not be presented as a confirmed death toll. The destruction itself, and its consequences for employment, are sufficient grounds for concern.
A March 5, 2025, Prothom Alo report recorded 95 permanent factory closures across major industrial areas during the preceding seven months, affecting 61,881 workers.
Its explanation extended beyond political violence: Financial distress, insufficient orders, attacks on politically-connected businesses, and owners going into hiding all contributed. The report identified 33,244 job losses across 14 factories in Beximco Industrial Park. These losses are included in the broader total and should not be counted as an additional figure.
This evidence supports criticism of inadequate protection and industrial disruption. However, it does not establish that every closure resulted from retaliation. Maintaining this distinction strengthens the argument by focusing attention on failures that authorities could reasonably have prevented or mitigated.
An owner accused of corruption should be subject to investigation, asset recovery where justified, and a fair trial. Employees, suppliers, and customers should not automatically lose their livelihoods or contracts.
Where legally permissible and commercially feasible, professional administration or restructuring can preserve a viable enterprise while the courts determine liability. These arrangements must protect creditors and prevent the concealment or diversion of assets.
Nor should the preservation of employment serve as a justification for rescuing every indebted conglomerate with public funds. Some businesses may be insolvent or reliant on privileges that cannot continue.
The objective should be orderly restructuring, transparent decision-making, and payment of workers’ lawful dues. Political identity should neither confer immunity nor substitute for evidence.
Achieving this requires decisions at the level of individual enterprises. Authorities should distinguish funds suspected of being criminal proceeds from those necessary for lawful operations. Restrictions should be justified, proportionate, and subject to review.
Workers need clear information on wages and compensation, while lenders require reliable financial statements and a viability assessment.
Without this discipline, a campaign against wrongdoing can spread losses throughout an entire supply chain and undermine confidence in legitimate enforcement.
The broader deterioration in public order reinforces this concern. In its year-end 2025 reporting, Ain o Salish Kendra recorded at least 197 deaths from mob violence during that year and reported at least 293 since the interim administration began.
The latter was a cumulative figure reported before that administration ended, not a final count for its entire tenure. These deaths demonstrate a serious failure of protection, although they cannot all be classified as political retaliation.
Human Rights Watch’s January 2025 report also documented the resurgence of abusive security practices and reprisals against individuals perceived to support the Awami League. Its warnings about arbitrary arrests and indiscriminate criminal complaints underscore the importance of due process.
Accountability loses credibility when allegations supplant investigation or when individuals are treated as guilty by association.
Economic consequences arise through identifiable channels. Damage to factories disrupts production and deliveries. Uncertain legal treatment may discourage lending and investment. Workers who lose wages reduce their spending, affecting shops, transport operators, and other local businesses.
These mechanisms provide compelling reasons to protect enterprises, although the World Bank’s aggregate figures do not quantify the distinct contribution of political retaliation.
The investment indicators are concerning. Private sector credit growth fell to its lowest level in 33 years. Net foreign direct investment declined by 15% in FY 2025-26, while new equity investment fell by 70. 3%.
Weakness in the financial sector, energy shortages, and global conditions also influence these outcomes. These figures are warning signs of a challenging investment environment, rather than evidence of a single political cause.
The earlier poverty assessment recorded nearly two million fewer employed people between 2023 and 2024 and projected a further decline of 0.8 million in 2025. That projection should not be treated as a subsequently verified outcome. Its broader message remains relevant: Weakening employment and purchasing power threaten households with limited capacity to absorb shocks.
There are also achievements to acknowledge. Remittances reached $35.6 billion in FY 2025-26, reserves improved, and average inflation eased from 10% to 8.7%.
More transparent recognition of problem loans is necessary, although the reported non-performing loan ratio of 33.2% in June 2026 demonstrates the scale of the remaining repair effort. Macroeconomic stabilization is valuable, but it must translate into productive investment and employment.
The elected government now bears responsibility for recovery. It should protect viable firms through lawful restructuring, investigate industrial arson regardless of political affiliation, and review cases through independent scrutiny of the evidence.
Bank restructuring requires credible deadlines and a fair allocation of losses. Reliable energy supply and stronger revenue collection should also form part of the recovery agenda.
Households need protection while these reforms take effect. About half of the poorest remain outside social protection programs. The World Bank estimates that consolidating food subsidies and combining the Family Card with better targeting of existing cash programs could lift millions out of poverty.
Bangladesh need not choose between justice and jobs. It must pursue justice through institutions capable of protecting both public funds and lawful livelihoods.
The promise of dignity after the uprising cannot be fulfilled if ordinary workers repeatedly bear the costs of their employers' politics.
The writer is a US-based policy analyst and freelance consultant on financial risk management.

item.title: Fazl clarifies he criticised policies, not institutions after ministers allege he sought 'share' in KP governance. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman on Saturday clarified that his party’s remarks regarding the country’s security situation were directed at policies, not institutions, and termed the allegations levelled against him by federal ministers as character assassination.

A day earlier, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, without naming anyone, had claimed that a “head of a party” was “extremely upset” about not being appointed the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The remarks came after Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights and raised doubts over its reasoning behind imposing governor’s rule that there was a lack of cooperation on counterterrorism.

Earlier on Saturday, State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry also rebuked the JUI-F chief for reportedly seeking his “share” in KP’s governance following the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province. Other federal ministers have also taken exception to Fazl’s remarks.

Addressing a press conference in Lahore on Saturday, Fazl stressed that his party’s criticism was directed at policies, not institutions, and was intended to bring about corrective action rather than undermine the sacrifices made in the fight against terrorism.

The senior politician called for an in-camera session of Parliament to review the country’s security situation and formulate a consensus-based policy to combat terrorism.

“Our only question is why the country has failed to eliminate terrorism. Let us sit together and find out why. Parliament is the most appropriate forum to discuss the issue and make decisions. Instead of ridiculing politicians, the government should take them on board in this fight so that we can move forward together,” he said.

“If Parliament is supreme, why are decisions taken in Rawalpindi while Parliament is simply told to follow them?” he remarked. “The issue is that this government is powerless. Decisions are taken somewhere else, and it implements them obediently,” he alleged.

The JUI-F maintained that Parliament should review the security situation and that the nation should be taken into confidence. If the public was expected to support the fight against terrorism and those engaged in it, he argued, the government should explain its decisions rather than impose “unilateral measures”.

Fazl reiterated his objection to the imposition of emergency rule in KP or any other part of the country. Recalling his family’s opposition to emergency rule in Balochistan during the 1970s, he said his father had resigned when the government of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto imposed it in the province.

He described the recurrence of such measures as unfortunate, pointing out that the PP had repeatedly been associated with their imposition.

Questioning the rationale behind the emergency, governor’s rule and deployment of troops in KP, Fazl asked why the province should face such treatment when Balochistan was also grappling with the same level of terrorist violence, if not more.

The JUI-F chief urged the government to develop a shared national narrative and a consensus-based counterterrorism strategy instead of questioning his party’s position.

He went on to ask why the government engaged in negotiations with the PTI, which had been in power in KP, if the party was accused of supporting terrorists. “On top of it, both (the PTI and the government) say that they had reached a consensus on all points.”

Fazl then highlighted that around 250 of his party workers had lost their lives in terrorist violence, arguing that their sacrifices should not be ridiculed or overlooked. “How can a party whose members have laid their lives be accused of supporting terrorists?” he asked.

He also questioned why he was being singled out for criticism when political leaders, including former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, had at various times disagreed with the military leadership.

Ministers assail Fazl

Earlier on Saturday, addressing the media in Jaranwala, Chaudhry said, “I am upset. We did not expect Maulana sahab […] to consider this as spoils of war and seek his share in the absence of a PTI government in the province.”

He emphasised that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was not a political move aimed at strengthening the PML-N’s presence in the province by dismissing the PTI-led government.

“This was an administrative setup,” he said, adding that it had been formed with a “one-point agenda: combating terrorism”, rather than with an intention of establishing a political setup.

“This is not spoils of war,” he reiterated, adding that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was an “immensely responsible” decision taken after every other option had been considered.

“I am unable to understand why Maulana sahab says that he was forced to accept defeat [in elections],” he said, arguing that Fazl’s party had been defeated by the PTI in KP and the Pashtunkhwa Milli Awami Party in Balochistan.

Chaudhry said the JUI-F was worthy of respect only if it stood by Pakistan’s interests.

The state minister also rejected the impression that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule was aimed at taking control of KP’s natural resources.

He also criticised Fazl for bringing up the 1971 separation of East Pakistan — now Bangladesh — from Pakistan in his recent statements.

“You bring up 1971 after losing the 2024 elections,” Chaudhry said.

“This KP setup is not about distributing shares, forming coalitions and governments, or engaging in politics,” he stressed, clarifying that only one member of the KP Advisory Council has a political background, as she represents the families of martyrs.

Chaudhry again offered to implement the National Action Plan and combat terrorism jointly with all stakeholders. “Politics is possible only where there is peace,” he said.

At the outset of his address, Chaudhry alleged that there must be “a relationship or a mutual interest arrangement between the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and the PTI”.

“Since 2015, no PTI leader, gathering or member has been targeted by terrorists,” Chaudhry said. “On the other hand, over the past 11 years, no political or religious party, security force, public office, funeral or wedding has been spared terrorist attacks.”

He said the federal government had exhausted all avenues to bring together stakeholders and urge them to condemn terrorism by naming those involved, whether the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), or groups funded by India or Afghanistan.

The state minister claimed that in 2013, when the government decided to hold talks with the TTP and representatives were proposed by both sides, the TTP had nominated PTI founder Imran Khan to its committee.

He also alleged that the PTI founder had allowed the TTP to open offices in Peshawar.

During his address, Chaudhry also criticised the PTI, showing a press release issued by the TTP that condemned the dismissal of the party’s government.

Meanwhile, speaking at a press conference in Sialkot, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif criticised the JUI-F chief for constantly “targeting” the country’s security forces.

He declared that the sacrifices made by the security forces, officers, and the public in the fight against terrorism were “matchless”.

The defence minister referred to Fazl’s accusations that the emergency and governor’s rule were imposed to capture KP’s mineral resources, saying that he had shared a full list of people who had the mining contracts in KP.

Asif maintained that the whole PTI and opposition leadership was engaged by the government before the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule.

“But it was fruitless,” he said.

“The situation will improve in KP […] parliament can roll back the decision of imposing the emergency only if the improvement of the situation in the province is guaranteed,” the defence minister said.

He said that some individuals in KP were expecting to get a share in the administrative changes in the province.

“We will ensure free and fair elections. Whenever the time comes, everybody can take part in it,” he said.

Fazl’s remarks also prompted a response from KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, who has now been tasked with running the province under governor’s rule.

Kundi, referring to the JUI-F chief, asked whether “your land in the land belonging to martyrs in DI Khan is halal”.

“What you get is halal, what the other gets is haram,” he remarked.

The governor reaffirmed that the new KP administration would continue to function properly.

‘Extremely upset’

Fazl, who was involved in reducing tensions between the Centre and the KP government, has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in KP. He also accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts to mediate between the two parties.

Addressing a rally in Multan on Thursday, Fazl further recalled that his party had expressed reservations over the merger of tribal areas into KP after the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018.

“We were not against the merger, but we said that it was an issue of the political future of the people of tribal areas,” he said, alleging that the people of those areas were not consulted on the merger.

He alleged governor’s rule was not imposed in Balochistan because the province’s chief minister “praises you”.

The next day, during an interaction with journalists, the interior minister said, “The head of a party is extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship.”

This politician, Naqvi alleged, had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”.

“These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged.

He said such politicians had little justification for criticising others now, particularly after having benefitted from the same system they currently denounced.

The same day, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz also railed against Fazl in a post on X.

She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitate terrorism — an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism.

She also criticised Fazl for his remarks about Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, seemingly referring to his comments during the Multan address about the centralisation of power.

The Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Oct 11, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.

The move has drawn criticism from the opposition, including Fazl, as well as Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan.

In the days preceding the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI which was in power in KP — had remained high since jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release.

Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results, while Fazl was cast as the man who could defuse heightening tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides had held separate meetings with Fazl, reportedly for his intervention to help break the deadlock in the negotiations.

item.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak, a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates.

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organisation said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year.

So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94 per cent of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said.

Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95pc, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped.

A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents.

“This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University.

Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said.

“The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said.

Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article.

‘They came only after i Buried my son’

In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived.

His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said.

Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition.

In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine.

“No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.

In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90pc, while second-dose coverage was 86pc, several percentage points below the 95pc needed for herd immunity.

The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025.

It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100pc of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

item.title: Doing all we can to reduce poverty. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As the world observed the International Day for Eradication of Poverty, it is clear that our national reflections must be anchored in sobering reality rather than complacent rhetoric.
The World Bank’s latest revelations -- confirming that our GDP growth has slumped to a dismal 3.4% and that over 2 million additional people have been pushed into poverty over the past year -- expose what must be identified as a profound socio-economic crisis.
For a nation that long aspired towards double digit growth, to have been reduced to below 4% for consecutive years is a significant blow. We must also contend with the fact that nearly 62 million citizens live just above the poverty line, meaning a single health shock, price spike, or market disruption can plunge entire families back into extreme hardship.
To that end, poverty eradication remains a distant dream for our country, and that is the reality. However, addressing it, and ensuring that we pull people out of poverty every day instead, is an urgent national emergency.
For too long, our poverty alleviation strategies have relied on fragmented, leaky safety programs that frequently miss the poorest segments of society while misallocating resources. While we are looking to change that narrative with the Family Card program, we must ensure that we get this right.
It goes without saying that a nation striving for structural reform can no longer tolerate a system where wealth inequality widens while the vulnerable absorb the harshest blows of economic stagnation.
Reducing poverty must go beyond merely managing destitution for our population. While the short term requires us to pull more and more people out of extreme poverty, the end goal must be to fix our macroeconomic foundations, drive job creation, and ensure that economic recovery lifts every citizen, not just a privileged few.
The end goal must always be to become an equitable nation, not merely a prosperous one.

item.title: Ending the culture of violence against journalists. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The killing of a journalist in Netrokona is another grim reminder of the dangers faced by those who investigate wrongdoing and bring uncomfortable truths to public attention.
Such attacks carry consequences that extend far beyond the individual victim: They threaten the public’s right to information and undermine the very foundations of accountability.
Lutfuzzaman Alif Fakir, a Netrokona correspondent for Ruposhi Bangla who frequently reported on corruption through his page Detective Article, was shot dead by unidentified assailants in Durgapur on Thursday night. He had previously survived a violent attack in November of last year.
This tragedy raises serious questions about whether adequate protective measures were taken following that prior incident.
It must be made clear: This culture of violence against journalists is completely unacceptable and must be brought under control.
The authorities must treat this killing with the urgency it demands. The perpetrators must be identified, arrested, and brought to justice through a prompt and transparent investigation.
Without accountability, those who resort to violence to silence the press will only feel emboldened.
However, seeking justice after a killing is not enough. Bangladesh urgently needs a proactive system to safeguard journalists before threats escalate into tragedy.
Complaints of intimidation and physical violence must be investigated immediately, backed by credible risk assessments and timely protection. Local law enforcement must take threats against reporters seriously -- especially when victims have already experienced violence.
Media organizations also share a duty to establish safety protocols, provide legal assistance, and stand by journalists facing danger due to their work. Freelancers and local correspondents, who often operate with limited institutional support, must not be left behind.
A free press cannot function when journalists are forced to choose between speaking the truth and preserving their lives. Nor can citizens expect corruption and abuse of power to be exposed if those who investigate them are left exposed to harm.
This tragedy must spur concrete action. Protecting journalists is nothing less than protecting democracy itself.

item.title: Memory as identity, memory as a file cabinet. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Recently, we lost a dear family friend who lived to the remarkable age of 100 years and 9 months. She attended our wedding back in the late 1970s, and we remained in touch over the years.
During the last two decades especially, we visited her frequently in Paris. Now that she is gone, our memories of her live on, providing us with a source of comfort and contentment, and serving as a kind of shock absorber as we come to terms with her loss.
She lived in Bangladesh as a UN official, and had contributed to the women’s developmental issues in the mid-1970s. Bangladesh had a special place in her heart. She would always read my pieces -- even after she turned 100 -- and share her comments when we called her for long chats. I always found her feedback thoughtful and uplifting.
She would also advise me to read something she discovered. Decades ago, she introduced me to the works of philosopher Rene Girard (1923-2015) -- almost her namesake; ours was Renee Gerard (1926-2026).
Remembering her company, advice, chats in her book-filled living room in Paris, or having a meal at a Parisian restaurant gave me the idea of writing on memories. Suddenly, I remembered what our English teacher KPC (Kali Prashad Chaterjee) at Bagerhat High School taught us when elucidating William Wordsworth’s poem The Daffodils. KPC, summarizing the poem, told us that you find joy twice: First, by seeing the daffodils in the lake, and then again by remembering them.
This is what human memory does. It is not an archive we consult but a place we return to -- and we come back changed, often with a smile on our face.
Imagine life without memory. Each moment would arrive without a past and depart without a future to hold it. We could still eat, work, and move through the day, but nothing would add up.
A life lived only in the now is a series of disjointed events, not a story. It is memory that turns events into a biography, and a biography into an identity. We know who we are because we remember who we have been, and whom we have been with.
Nowhere is this clearer than in grief. When someone we love dies, what remains is not a file but a relationship that continues inside us. I remember my mother's laughter while reading Shibram Chakraborty, or Syed Mujtaba Ali. I remember a teacher's scolding, or a rare, hard-won praise.
These memories hurt, yet they also hold us. They remind us that we were loved, that we belonged somewhere, that someone's life was woven into ours.
Mourning is, in large part, the slow work of converting an absence into a memory we can live with. The dead do not leave us entirely so long as we remember them, and in remembering them we remember ourselves.
Memory also gives us a sense of direction. We recall the choices that led us here, the sacrifices others made, the values we were handed and the ones we chose. From these we draw purpose. A person who remembers a parent's quiet persistence may find the strength to persist. A person who remembers a friend's generosity may decide to be generous.
Human memory is also practical. We use it to solve problems, to recall what Marx said and where -- “peasants are like potatoes in a sack” in the Eighteenth Brumaire -- as students remain impressed. Memory helps us learn, plan, and function. In this respect, it resembles the memory of a computer, which also stores information and retrieves it when needed.
The comparison is tempting, and it is useful as far as it goes. Both kinds of memory help a system get things done.
But the parallel ends there. A computer's memory is functional through and through. It stores data in order to process it, and it retrieves data in order to complete a task. When a hard drive holds 10,000 photographs, none of them is more precious than another unless a program is told to rank them. Nothing in the machine aches when a file is deleted. Nothing is consoled when a file is restored. The memory serves the operation and has no stake in what it holds.
The newest AI systems, for all their astonishing fluency, do not change this. They can recall vast amounts of information, summarize a life, even write a convincing elegy. They can store and retrieve what we tell them about our parents.
Yet storing is not remembering.
There is, as far as we can tell, no one inside who is comforted by the retrieval, no one for whom the stored detail is a loss or a gift. These systems generate words about meaning without, so far as we know, experiencing meaning.
Their memory is a tool. Ours is a part of who we are.
There is a quiet lesson here about how we live: If memory is where meaning is made, then we have a responsibility to tend to it. We can ask our elders for their stories before it is too late. We can name the people who shaped us and tell their stories to the young. We can resist the thin, hurried present in which nothing is remembered because nothing is allowed to matter.
A culture that stops remembering together -- in rituals, anniversaries, and family tables -- will find that it has plenty of data and very little meaning.
At its core, computer memory is a vast digital filing system built on billions of microscopic electronic switches called transistors, but it has no emotion, least consciousness. Its functional power lies in speed and exact replication: It can store billions of these tiny data points, execute complex calculations, and retrieve files with absolute precision in nanoseconds without ever degrading, misremembering, or imbuing a single byte with emotion.
Computers will keep getting better at storing everything. What they cannot do, at least for now, is care about what they store.
That is our work, and also our gift. We remember -- not only to function, but to belong, to grieve, to love, and to go on.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: A card is not a safety net if the poor remain invisible. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A garment worker loses her job. A riverbank family is displaced. A widow suddenly becomes the sole provider for her children. Their circumstances can change overnight; a government beneficiary list may not.
That time lag is not just a clerical inconvenience. For a household already choosing between food and medicine, a temporary hardship can turn into lasting poverty.
This is why Bangladesh's latest social protection exercise deserves more scrutiny than the excitement surrounding a new card.
On October 12, the government began nationwide door-to-door collection of household information for the Family Card program. Officials say the database is intended to cover approximately 45 million households, with data collection due to conclude on November 30.
It is an ambitious administrative undertaking. But its success will depend less on the number of entries gathered than on the number of vulnerable families no longer falling through the cracks.
The World Bank's October 2026 Bangladesh Development update offers a sobering benchmark. It estimates that the number of people living in poverty increased by approximately 2.1 million in FY2025-26, while about half of the poorest households remain outside social protection programs.
These findings should be read together. At precisely the moment when more families need a cushion, the existing system struggles to reach many who are already at the bottom.
For too long, our public conversation has treated social protection as a contest of allocations: How many schemes, how many beneficiaries, how many billions of taka. Those figures matter, but they cannot establish whether assistance is timely, adequate, or fairly targeted.
A benefit announced is not necessarily a benefit received; a name on a list is not an assurance of future eligibility; and a card in a wallet does not, by itself, protect a family against the next shock.
The central policy challenge is what economists call exclusion error: Households that qualify for assistance are left out.
At the same time, inclusion errors can direct scarce resources to those who do not qualify. Perfect targeting is impossible, but both forms of error can be measured and reduced.
The new exercise relies on a proxy means test to estimate household welfare from observable characteristics. That is more systematic than selection by discretion alone, yet a score cannot fully capture a sudden dismissal, an expensive illness, or the loss of land to a river. A statistical estimate should guide an eligibility decision, not make it immune to challenge.
An announced benefit is not necessarily a benefit received; a card in a wallet is not protection against the next shock.
The government's stated plan to receive appeals online and through union parishad service centres is therefore important. But an appeal mechanism is meaningful only if it works for people with limited literacy, poor connectivity, or no local influence.
Applicants should receive intelligible reasons for rejection, a tracking number, and a decision within a published period. Independent spot checks and public reporting on overturned decisions could separate a functioning grievance system from a mere box for collecting complaints.
Even a carefully constructed database can become obsolete. A household above the eligibility threshold today may fall below it after an illness, a price shock, or river erosion.
Bangladesh needs its planned dynamic social registry to work as a continuously updated public service, rather than a one-off enumeration exercise.
Households must be able to report changes without incurring expensive travel or relying on unofficial intermediaries. In disaster-affected localities, rapid reassessments should be possible without waiting for another nationwide survey.
This matters particularly in the informal economy, where fluctuating earnings rarely appear in conventional employment records.
Program design poses a second challenge. Issuing the Family Card in a woman's name is a potentially valuable recognition of her economic agency. Yet, deprivation is not identical for every member of a household.
An older person requiring care, a person with a disability, and a child facing malnutrition need different combinations of services. Integrating databases and eliminating unnecessary duplication are sensible objectives.
Replacing every specialized program with an undifferentiated household payment would not be sensible. The goal should be a common gateway to appropriately tailored support.
Privacy must be treated as a condition of inclusion, not an afterthought. A registry on this scale will contain sensitive information about identities, assets, and family circumstances. Without safeguards, it could expose vulnerable people to data misuse or unjust exclusion.
Information collection should be proportionate to need, access restricted to official roles, changes auditable, and errors correctable by the households concerned. Program performance should be transparent; recipients' private circumstances should not be.
There will be a familiar objection: Bangladesh cannot afford administrative perfection while its budget is under strain. The fiscal constraint is real.
According to the World Bank, revenue collection stood at only 8.3% of GDP in FY2025-26, and economic growth is projected at 3.4% in FY2026-27. Yet scarcity strengthens the case for accuracy.
Every avoidable duplicate payment, unresolved exclusion, or delayed transfer carries a higher social cost when the fiscal room for correction is so narrow. Better targeting is not a substitute for adequate funding; it is a way to improve the impact of that funding.
Indeed, the World Bank estimates that, under a reform scenario combining better-targeted existing cash programs, food-subsidy consolidation, and the Family Card, an additional 2.85 million people could be lifted out of poverty, and this is a modelled possibility, not an assured outcome.
It nevertheless illustrates why the quality of implementation matters. Nor should the reform agenda be reduced to austerity. Removing subsidies before dependable compensation reaches vulnerable households would shift the burden of adjustment onto those least able to bear it.
A credible reform program should publish a modest set of results every quarter: The share of the poorest households receiving assistance, the time between approval and first payment, the proportion of grievances resolved, payment failure rates, and whether women can access transfers without intermediaries.
District-level comparisons, with appropriate privacy safeguards, would help locate persistent gaps. An independent evaluation after the first year would reveal far more than a ceremony celebrating cards distributed.
Ultimately, social protection is about the relationship between citizens and the state. A fair system does not require a family to prove its desperation repeatedly or to rely on familiarity with an official. It recognizes vulnerability, responds when circumstances change, and explains decisions that affect people's lives.
Bangladesh has an opportunity to make the Family Card more than another symbol of welfare reform. The next milestone should not simply be the completion of a national database. It should be the moment when an eligible household can trust that need, rather than connections or procedural luck, determines access to assistance.
A safety net earns its name not when a card is issued, but when someone falling is actually caught.
Dr Munshi Muhammad Abdul Kader Jilani holds a PhD in Knowledge Management from Wuhan University of Technology in China. He is currently working as an Assistant Professor at the Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM), University of Dhaka (Affiliated), and Associate Editor of the BIGM Journal of Policy Analysis.

item.title: Indian police detain 'cockroach' movement founder Dipke ahead of protest. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Police detained India’s ‘cockroach’ movement founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday, live images from his group showed, ahead of a protest called by him in capital Delhi’s central business district, the latest rally to demand the resignation of India’s election chief.

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), opposition groups, and student organisations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.

Dipke called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.

The group and left-wing student organisations had urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi’s busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag.

The live video on CJP’s Instagram handle showed Dipke coming out of a house and walking towards the street, where police officers stopped him and, after a brief argument, hauled him into a police car and drove away.

“We are detaining you right now,” a police officer could be heard telling Dipke.

“I have not broken any law right now…how can you detain me?” Dipke asked the police officers as he was taken away.

There was no immediate comment from the police on the detention.

Earlier on Friday, police met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest.

Park closed ahead of protest

Authorities closed the central New Delhi park before the protest over the voter-roll revision, which critics say has disenfranchised millions.

Dipke urged supporters to rally at Central Park after two of his colleagues were detained for breaching security barricades at Jantar Mantar, where they had gone to wave the national flag.

Earlier this week, police removed authorisation for Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.

On Friday, thousands of security personnel were deployed in parts of the city, with yellow-coloured metal barricades put up at key intersections.

Earlier, Dipke said he was undeterred despite the possibility of being arrested ahead of Friday’s protest.

“Why are you so afraid of cockroaches?” Dipke said.

“I want to tell Narendra Modi that we are not afraid… if waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready,” he said Thursday.

Delhi’s municipal authorities said they were closing the Central Park for two days for “administrative” reasons.

Delhi Police have barred public gatherings around Connaught Place citing concerns about public order and safety.

Violation of the orders would “attract suitable legal action”, police said Thursday, but added that they would allow “selected persons” to gather at a “suitable place”.

In recent days, the Indian capital has seen street protests over a large-scale voter roll revision exercise overseen by chief election commissioner Kumar.

Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.

Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.

On Friday, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh dismissed the allegations, saying the sole agenda of the opposition parties was “to destroy democratic institutions and create unrest in the country”.

“Their fight is not for electoral reform… not for Gyanesh Kumar, not for the bright future of the country’s youth,” he said at a news conference.

“Rather, this is their conspiracy to seize power by creating anarchy in the country.”

item.title: Afghanistan produce thrilling rearguard to save Bangladesh Test. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Sediqullah Atal’s marathon century and some inspired lower-order resistance inspired Afghanistan to a dramatic draw in the one-off Test against Bangladesh on Tuesday.

Opener Atal, playing only his third Test, batted for eight-and-a-half hours for his 332-ball 111 before number nine Qais Ahmad hit an unbeaten 49 in Abu Dhabi.

Having started the final day on 132-3, Afghanistan survived to finish on 346-8, from a total of 142 overs, after being set a nominal 479-run target to win.

When Atal fell to a close-in catch off left-arm spinner Taijul Islam soon after tea with the score at 281-7, Bangladesh were in sight of victory.

But Qais and fellow tail-ender Yamin Ahmadzai (19 off 85 balls) batted for 110 deliveries in a valiant 45-run stand for the eighth wicket to resist Bangladesh’s spinners.

Even when Ahmadzai fell to Mehidy Hasan Miraz, Bangladesh had five overs to enforce a win but Qais and number 10 Zia-ur-Rehman hung on, although not without drama.

There were two missed run-out chances in the final session and a dropped catch, while Qais gave his team-mates watching from the boundary some heart-stopping moments.

The leg-spinner mixed solid defence with a penchant for dancing down the pitch, even hitting the second ball of the last over for six.

The Bangladesh players were less than impressed with Qais when he went down with an apparent hamstring injury and received treatment after playing a forward defence with 10 minutes remaining.

With a famous draw already secured, he hammered the final delivery of the match deep over midwicket for another maximum, falling to the turf in celebration.

Pacer Ebadot Hossain took 3-50 and off-spinner Miraz finished with 3-73, but it was not enough for Bangladesh.

Bangladesh skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto praised Afghanistan’s resilience.

“It is disappointing not win, but Afghanistan played brilliantly,” said Shanto. “I expected the spinners to come into the match. They tried but Afghanistan played very good cricket.”

Sediqullah earlier reached his century with a boundary off Hasan Mahmud, becoming the first Afghanistan batter to reach three figures in the fourth innings of a Test.

Hashmatullah Shahidi also scored 36 and helped Atal defy the Bangladesh bowling, but holed out to mid-on attempting a big shot down the ground, just seven minutes before tea.

Ismat Alam batted for 60 deliveries for his four — scoring his first run off his 44th delivery — before Miraz had him caught by Shanto.

With under two hours left, Bangladesh were finally rewarded with Sediqullah’s wicket as the left-hander pushed a turning delivery from Islam and a thick edge was well caught at short-leg by Tanzid Hasan.

But the exploits of Ahmadzai, Qais and Zia ensured the Afghans had the last say.
